title: The Genevan psalter
hookLine: Calvin's churches sang the psalms set to rhyme and tune

lines: MAKE A JOYFUL NOISE, ALL YE LANDS.
RHYME AND METER, ONE STRONG TUNE.
cards: Psalm one hundred, in the King James Bible: "Make a joyful noise unto the LORD, all ye lands. Serve the LORD with gladness: come before his presence with singing." Lovely.
Now try getting a whole church to sing that together: farmers, children, people who can't read. Prose has no steady beat. Nobody knows when to breathe or where the tune goes next.
In Geneva, John Calvin's church found an answer: put the psalms into rhyme and regular meter, so anyone could sing them to one strong tune. Today's word: metrical psalm.

teach.h: A PSALM IN RHYME AND METER.
teach.b: A metrical psalm is a psalm rewritten in rhymed verse, with a regular count of syllables in each line, so it fits a tune.

Calvin wanted the whole congregation singing in worship, not only trained singers. And for songs to sing to God, he argued, you could not do better than the psalms, words he believed God's Spirit had already given.
So poets set the psalms into French verse, and musicians fitted them to simple, sturdy tunes. The result was the Genevan Psalter. The idea traveled.

teach.h: ALL PEOPLE THAT ON EARTH DO DWELL.
teach.b: English Protestants who had lived in Geneva carried it home, and one of them, William Kethe, set Psalm one hundred like this: "All people that on earth do dwell, / Sing to the Lord with cheerful voice."

Eight syllables a line. That steady count lets a crowd move together, breathing in the same places. His words were sung to a tune from the Genevan psalter, and the pairing came to be called the Old Hundredth.
Kept from the psalm: all ye lands becomes all people on earth; gladness becomes a cheerful voice. Changed: now it rhymes, and a child can remember it after a few Sundays.

Paul told the Colossians to be "teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord." Churches read that line in more than one way.
Some Reformed and Presbyterian churches sing only psalms in worship. Others sing psalms alongside hymns.

teach.h: THE BIBLE'S SONGBOOK, IN ORDINARY MOUTHS.
teach.b: Either way, the metrical psalm put the Bible's own songbook into ordinary mouths.

how: Reformed and Presbyterian churches sing metrical psalms from psalters, some singing only psalms in worship and others mixing psalms with hymns; "All people that on earth do dwell" to the Old Hundredth tune is sung in churches of several traditions.

games.q: you're a pastor in Geneva. you have Psalm 100 in prose and a church full of farmers, children and people who can't read. how do you get them all singing it?
o: have a trained choir sing it for them.
set it in rhyme and steady meter, to one strong tune.
have one person read it aloud while everyone listens.
games.why: Calvin's churches put the psalms into rhymed verse and fitted them to tunes. one English version became "All people that on earth do dwell."

practice: If you know the tune, sing the first two lines of the Old Hundredth, all people that on earth do dwell, sing to the Lord with cheerful voice; if not, say them slowly and tap the eight beats of each line on your knee.
Then sit in the quiet after the last note. If you pray, let the two lines be your prayer; if you don't, notice what it's like to put your one voice into words whole rooms have sung together.

wordCard.voice: Metrical psalm. A psalm set in rhyme and steady meter, so a whole congregation can sing it to one tune.

orig.note: Hebrew: a psalm, a song sung to music. Psalm 100 opens mizmor l'todah, "a psalm of praise" in the King James heading.

carryVoice: Your line: all people that on earth. One steady beat, and a whole room can sing. See you tomorrow.
